extracted.intended_audience: workers, employers, labor advocates, trade associations, and legal practitioners interested in FLSA employee vs independent contractor classification
extracted.subtask_description: Determining whether a worker is an FLSA-covered employee or an independent contractor using the multifactor economic-reality test and related Department and judicial guidance. Applies to rulemaking, enforcement, and legal analysis of classification across industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic reality / totality-of-the-circumstances test
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate inquiry is whether the worker is economically dependent on the employer for work or is in business for themself; the economic realities of the relationship are determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department apply a multifactor, totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test; no factor is dispositive and the list of factors is not exhaustive. Analyses should consider the "circumstances of the whole activity."

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which services are an integral part of the employer's business (the "integral part" factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the services rendered are an integral part of the alleged employer's business—e.g., whether the worker's tasks are part of the integrated unit of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically a key Silk/Rutherford factor; Department warns this is "different from the concept of the importance or centrality of the individual's work to the potential employer's business." Some circuits treat this differently (e.g., Fifth Circuit typically does not list it but still considers it); courts evaluate it as part of the total situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker's opportunity for profit or loss
rubrics_metrics.description: The worker's opportunity to earn profits or incur losses, depending on their exercise of initiative, managerial skill, business acumen, or by managing investments (helpers, equipment, materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 2021 IC Rule this was a core factor indicating independent contractor status when tied to initiative or investment management; the worker need not demonstrate both initiative and investment. Conversely, this factor indicates employee status to the extent the worker cannot affect earnings except by working more hours or faster. Some circuits combine this factor with investment; others treat them separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of the worker's investment in facilities, equipment, or materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative investments of the employer and worker in facilities, equipment, materials, or helpers required for the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as a separate factor in many formulations (WHD, MSPA, AI 2015-1). The Department's proposed rule would restore investment as a separate factor (distinct from profit/loss) and consider relative investments in assessing economic independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and degree of control exercised by the putative employer
rubrics_metrics.description: The alleged employer's right or exercise of control over the manner in which the work is performed, including scheduling, supervision, price-setting, and the worker's ability to work for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally included in Silk-derived lists; courts and the Department caution that control should not be the sole criterion. The 2021 IC Rule designated control as a "core factor" weighted more heavily; it also stated that requiring compliance with legal obligations, health and safety standards, insurance, contractual deadlines, or business-like quality controls does not constitute control for classification purposes. The NPRM proposes additional detailed analysis of control (scheduling, supervision, price-setting, ability to work for others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of initiative, judgment, foresight, or special skill required
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the services rendered require special skill, initiative, judgment, or foresight for success of an independent enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the Silk/Rutherford factors and echoed in WHD, MSPA, and later guidance; often described as informing whether the worker operates a separate business or is dependent on the employer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of permanency and duration of the working relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of permanence or the duration and stability of the relationship between the worker and the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered in Silk/Rutherford and subsequent WHD guidance (e.g., permanency of the relation). Used to gauge whether a worker is economically dependent on a single business or engaged in transient/independent business activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of independent business organization and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker has an independent business structure or operation—e.g., organized operations, ability to advertise, hold themselves out, or employ others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in WHD opinion letters and Fact Sheets as an additional consideration; treated as an indicium of being in business for oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual practice of the parties over written or contractual terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual day-to-day working relationship and practices are more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible; a written contract does not always reflect the true situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WHD guidance cautions that classification cannot ordinarily be made absent evidence of actual working relationship; courts look to practice and operations rather than labels in agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Suffer or permit" statutory standard (section 3(g) of the FLSA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FLSA's "suffer or permit" language provides an expansive scope of employment that is broader than common-law master-servant concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have cited the broad statutory language when applying the economic reality test; agencies treat the statutory phrasing as justifying a more expansive inquiry into economic dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single factor is controlling / non-exhaustive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and Department guidance repeatedly emphasize that no single factor or combination of factors invariably predominates and that the listed factors are not exhaustive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts must apply factors flexibly and avoid mechanical application; consider the total situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2021 IC Rule's five-factor framework with two designated "core factors"
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2021 Independent Contractor Rule identified five economic realities factors and designated two—(1) nature and degree of control and (2) opportunity for profit or loss—as "core factors" that should carry greater weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2021 Rule stated that if both core factors indicate the same classification, there is a "substantial likelihood" that the classification is correct. The Rule also acknowledged factors are not exhaustive and that actual practice matters; the 2021 Rule further provided illustrative examples. The Department later rescinded and/or proposed to replace the core-factor weighting with a return to totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2021 IC Rule's guidance on what does not constitute control
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 2021 Rule, requiring the worker to comply with legal obligations, satisfy health and safety standards, carry insurance, meet contractual deadlines or quality-control standards, or other terms typical of business contracts did not constitute control for classification purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a specific limiting instruction in the 2021 Rule that narrowed the scope of facts treated as employer control; the NPRM criticized aspects of the 2021 Rule as inconsistent with longstanding case law and proposed restoring a broader consideration of control (including scheduling, supervision, price-setting, and the ability to work for others).

rubrics_metrics.name: MSPA / sector-specific multifactor application
rubrics_metrics.description: For Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act (MSPA) cases, the ultimate question is economic dependence, evaluated by circumstances including: control, opportunity for profit or loss, investment, special skill, permanency, and integration into the employer's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSPA regulation (1997) mirrors the six-factor economic reality approach; though sector-specific, it illustrates application of the totality test in agriculture and incorporation of FLSA's "suffer or permit" standard by reference.
